subject: Agriculture
title: Mesopotamian Irrigation
description: A fast breakdown of Mesopotamian Irrigation for builders.

hook.text: Mesopotamia gets little rain. Without irrigation, the cradle of civilization would have been a desert.

buildup.text: Sumerians dug canals from the Tigris and Euphrates to carry water miles into dry fields.

discovery.text: Irrigated fields produced enormous wheat and barley harvests—enough to support the world's first cities.

twist.text: Irrigation brought salt. Over centuries, salt accumulated in the soil, killing crops and collapsing yields.

climax.text: Salinization ruined southern Mesopotamia's farmland. Some scholars say it ended Sumerian civilization.

punchline.text: Irrigation built empires. Salt buried them.

quiz.question: What long-term problem did irrigation cause in Mesopotamia?
options: Salt buildup in the soil that destroyed farmland

details.summary: Mesopotamian irrigation systems transformed the arid land between the Tigris and Euphrates into one of the most productive agricultural regions in history. This topic covers canal networks, water management, and how irrigation enabled the first civilizations but also led to salinization.
details.whyItMatters: Mesopotamia invented large-scale irrigation but also suffered its consequences. The eventual salinization of irrigated land offers an ancient warning about unsustainable water management.
takeaways: Mesopotamians built extensive canal systems to bring river water to fields
Irrigation enabled two harvests per year in otherwise desert conditions
Centuries of irrigation caused salt buildup that eventually degraded farmland

faq.question: How did Mesopotamians irrigate their farmland?
faq.answer: They constructed networks of canals, levees, and distribution channels to divert water from the Tigris and Euphrates rivers onto surrounding fields. Sluice gates controlled water flow, and maintenance crews kept channels clear of silt.

faq.question: What caused the decline of Mesopotamian agriculture?
faq.answer: Centuries of irrigation without proper drainage caused salts dissolved in river water to accumulate in topsoil. This salinization gradually reduced crop yields, forced shifts from wheat to more salt-tolerant barley, and ultimately degraded the land.
